parts.given_text: Between parallel plates the field magnitude is V/d. A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force.

sup-59a633a1a2b93971-q27:whole.hint: Identify the potential change along the particle’s actual path and keep the sign of its charge.
notes: In a uniform electric field, F = qE and a = qE/m. Across a potential change, ΔE_k = −qΔV if the electric force is the only force doing work.
Between parallel plates, |E| = |ΔV|/d away from edge effects. Do not use the entire plate-to-plate voltage for a particle that crosses only part of the gap.

notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).

sup-7b98eef406c31dfd-w6:a.hint: Find the angle between the conventional current and the magnetic field.
notes: A straight current-carrying segment experiences F = BIL sin θ. Use the length actually within the field.
Use the current direction for the force hand rule. The magnetic force is perpendicular to both current and field; a segment parallel to the field has no magnetic force.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-7b98eef406c31dfd-w6:b.hint: Identify the geometry producing the field before choosing its formula or hand rule.
notes: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); for a long ideal solenoid, B = μ₀nI. Here n is turns per unit length.
Use a right-hand grip rule with conventional current. Add fields as vectors, including cancellation between competing contributions.

sup-7b98eef406c31dfd-w6:c.i.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.
notes: Changing flux can drive induced current. Its magnetic effect opposes that flux change, transferring mechanical energy into electrical heating.
Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.

sup-7b98eef406c31dfd-w6:c.ii.hint: Look for a change in magnetic flux linkage, not just the presence of a magnetic field.
notes: Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ for a uniform field, with θ measured from the surface normal. Faraday’s law is ε = −N dΦ/dt.
A changing field, area or orientation can induce an emf. On a flux–time graph use the gradient; a large constant flux by itself gives no emf.
